name: InfraDispatch
problem: Pickup plans are often split across messages, spreadsheets and personal notes, so trip details, people, vehicles, costs and approvals can fall out of sync.
solution: A single rule-based workflow that turns operating inputs into an approved pickup plan, route links, team briefs, manifests and printable handover outputs.
why: Reduce missed handovers, duplicate coordination and last-minute uncertainty while giving supervisors one reviewable operating picture.
how: Enter the trip and team, add pickup and drop-off points, record costs, review the decision, approve the plan, then export the operational brief.
when: Use it before city tours, airport transfers, event movements and any multi-stop operation that needs coordinated guide, driver and vehicle assignments.
role: I defined the operating rules, information architecture, review gates, interface and static demonstration workflow.
outcome: The demonstration shows how one governed plan can replace fragmented coordination and make supervisor review easier before field handover.
limitations: Static MVP using mock or browser-local data. It has no live fleet API, authentication, database or production dispatch integration.

name: InfraCluster
problem: Large hotel pickup lists become difficult to operate when location, guest count, luggage, language, pickup windows and vehicle capacity are planned separately.
solution: A clustering workflow that groups hotels into practical operating zones, flags capacity pressure and prepares a clean dispatch handoff to InfraDispatch.
why: Make vehicle splits and pickup sequences easier to explain, review and cost before the movement reaches the dispatch team.
how: Set the service context, add hotels and guest requirements, compare proposed clusters, review vehicle fit and cost signals, then approve the preferred split.
when: Use it for MICE groups, multi-hotel city tours, airport movements and any service where several pickup points must be consolidated into workable routes.
role: I translated hotel-pickup constraints into a reviewable clustering method, capacity checks and dispatch-ready output.
outcome: The demonstration makes route grouping, capacity pressure and the reason for each proposed split visible to an operations reviewer.
limitations: Static MVP with illustrative clustering rules. It does not use live traffic, mapping optimisation or production booking data.

name: InfraSky
problem: Stargazing and desert experiences can be oversold when moon phase, visibility, haze, access, camp readiness and guest comfort are considered too late or in isolation.
solution: A condition-aware planner that converts supplied conditions into a sell, watch, avoid or block decision with safer guest wording and field briefings.
why: Protect guest trust and operational credibility by aligning the sales promise with conditions the guide, driver and camp team can realistically support.
how: Choose the date and product, enter the available sky and field conditions, review the readiness score, then use the generated sales copy, guide notes and checklist.
when: Use it before selling, confirming or operating stargazing tours, astronomy programmes, desert dinners and other condition-sensitive outdoor products.
role: I designed the condition model, decision language, readiness scoring and the handover between product promise and field delivery.
outcome: The demonstration shows how a product team can make a bounded sell, watch, avoid or block decision from supplied operating conditions.
limitations: Static MVP using user-supplied conditions. It does not claim live weather, astronomy, access or safety data.

name: InfraQuote
problem: Tour quotations become risky when guest requirements, supplier costs, vehicle assumptions, tickets, VAT, margin and client terms live in separate calculations.
solution: A controlled quotation workflow that separates the internal cost view from client output while checking break-even logic, margin and readiness warnings.
why: Protect commercial discipline, reduce hidden-cost mistakes and make every client price easier to review before it leaves the business.
how: Capture the request, build the cost worksheet, validate assumptions, review break-even and margin, resolve warnings, then generate the client-facing quotation.
when: Use it for new enquiries, custom itineraries, group quotations, supplier-price changes and every pre-approval review before a proposal is sent.
role: I structured the quotation journey, commercial calculations, internal controls and separation between cost review and client output.
outcome: The demonstration makes pricing assumptions and warnings inspectable before a client-facing quotation is generated.
limitations: Static MVP with browser-local calculations. It has no live supplier rates, accounting integration, tax service or approval database.
